title: Shock = delivery failure
body: Shock is inadequate perfusion, not a BP number.
Pump fails → cardiogenic. Pipes too wide → distributive. Fluid lost → hypovolemic.
Something squeezing or blocking the pump → obstructive.
On any scenario, ask: which part of the system broke?

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: The plumbing math
body: CO = HR × SV
BP = CO × SVR
Pulse pressure = SBP − DBP
MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓ pulse pressure
Stroke volume depends on preload, contractility, and afterload.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Why BP lies
body: Baroreceptors trigger a sympathetic surge: faster rate, stronger squeeze, vasoconstriction.
Hormones (RAAS, ADH) hold onto fluid; blood is shunted from skin and gut to core organs.
The body can hide about 25% volume loss behind a normal BP.
Early signs: tachycardia, anxiety. BP drops late, often past 30% loss.
Best brain-perfusion indicator: level of consciousness.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Cellular collapse
body: No oxygen → anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid.
ATP runs out → the sodium/potassium pump fails → cells swell and self-digest.
Acid and CO₂ buildup dilate vessels, undoing compensation.
End state: multiple-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS), often hours to days later.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Telling the types apart
body: Hypovolemic: cool, pale, clammy · tachycardic · flat neck veins.
Cardiogenic: cool, clammy · brady or tachy · JVD.
Obstructive: cool, clammy · tachycardic · JVD.
Distributive: usually warm · rate varies · flat neck veins.
Discriminators: skin temperature, then neck veins plus lung sounds.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Distributive subtypes
body: Septic: infection; skin often warm or hot despite shock.
Neurogenic: spinal injury; hypotension WITHOUT tachycardia, warm dry skin below the injury.
Anaphylactic: vasodilation plus bronchospasm; epinephrine is the only reversing treatment.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Obstructive subtypes
body: Tamponade: Beck's triad = JVD, muffled heart tones, narrowing pulse pressure.
Tension pneumo: needs needle decompression; tracheal deviation is late. Be careful with positive pressure.
PE: 250 mL bolus, recheck BP, repeat if SBP stays under 90.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Three stages
body: Compensated: BP held, pulse pressure narrowing, up to ~25% loss. Usually recoverable.
Decompensated: BP falling, >30% loss. Sometimes recoverable.
Irreversible: terminal.
You can't tell decompensated from irreversible in the field, so treat everyone aggressively.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

title: Shock recognition and management (RI 2.20A)
body: RI 2.20A is one protocol covering SIX shock states: undifferentiated, hypovolemic, obstructive, cardiogenic, septic and neurogenic.
General recognition: restlessness, confusion, pale and cool clammy skin, a weak rapid pulse, and hypotension — SBP < 90 or MAP < 65.
The third trigger is the one people forget: a SHOCK INDEX (heart rate ÷ systolic BP) of ≥ 0.6. That fires before the pressure falls, which is the whole point of calculating it.
Hypovolemic: a history of volume loss — vomiting, diarrhea, bleeding.
Obstructive: chest trauma, JVD, absent breath sounds, narrow pulse pressure, DVT history or pulmonary embolus risk factors.
Cardiogenic: STEMI, heart failure, dysrhythmias, bradycardia or tachycardia.
Neurogenic: spinal cord injury with hypotension, and warm dry skin with a normal or BRADYCARDIC rate — the opposite of the tachycardia you expect in shock.
Septic: fever, warm skin, tachycardia, tachypnea, a possible source of infection.

Management: routine patient care; keep the patient supine if tolerated; maintain and promote NORMOTHERMIA with blankets and by raising the ambient temperature; transport to the nearest appropriate facility.

Suspected OBSTRUCTIVE shock is managed by its cause, not by this protocol — RI sends you to the etiology-specific protocol, giving the Multiple Trauma Protocol for a suspected tension pneumothorax as the example.
If adrenal insufficiency is suspected, run the Adrenal Insufficiency Protocol alongside this one.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Shock fluids: which fluid, how much, to what target
body: WHICH FLUID (RI 1.01 §14): 0.9% saline is the fluid of choice for keep-vein-open purposes and limited boluses. Lactated Ringer's is the fluid of choice for SIGNIFICANT fluid resuscitation in shock and burn injury, unless a protocol directs otherwise.
HOW MUCH (RI 2.20A): lactated Ringer's 500 mL IV, repeated to reach the target, to a MAXIMUM OF 2 LITRES.
THE TARGET is a number, not "looks better": SBP ≥ 100 or MAP ≥ 65. Note the gap — you RECOGNISE shock below SBP 90, but you RESUSCITATE to 100.
Past 2 litres, fluid is no longer the answer and vasopressors enter the protocol — push-dose epinephrine 10–20 mcg IV every 3–5 minutes is the first of several options listed, at levels above AEMT.
KVO rates are specified: 20–30 mL/hour for adults, 10–20 mL/hour for pediatrics.
Hemorrhagic shock has its OWN protocol (2.21A) rather than being managed here — bleeding control changes the arithmetic.
An intermittent needle therapy device (saline lock) may replace an infusing IV when appropriate.
RI states plainly that IO access is interchangeable with IV throughout these protocols, and that any reference to the IV route includes the IO route.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Exam traps
body: Normal BP does not rule out shock.
Bradycardia + hypotension: think cardiogenic or neurogenic, then check skin temp.
Don't wait for late signs (tracheal deviation, cyanosis).
Check SBP and get IV access before nitro in any possible cardiogenic patient.
Elderly hypertensive patients can be in shock with SBP above 100.
RI 4.01A: SBP <110 in a patient over 65 may already be shock.

source.doc: Chapter 14 - Shock AEMT-C Study Guide

conflicts.nremt: SBP >90 and IV access first

title: Shock fluids, RI protocol detail
body: Shock = SBP <90, MAP <65, or shock index (HR ÷ SBP) ≥0.6.
General shock (2.20A): LR 500 mL, repeat to SBP ≥100 or MAP ≥65.
External hemorrhage (2.21A): control the bleeding first, then LR 500 mL to SBP ≥90 or MAP ≥65, max 2 L.
Penetrating torso, no TBI: LR 250 mL, repeat only to a radial pulse, SBP ~80, or normal mentation, max 2 L.
Penetrating torso with TBI: LR 250–500 mL to SBP ≥90 (the brain needs pressure).
Peds (2.20P/2.21P): LR 20 mL/kg (10 mL/kg under 3 months), max 60 mL/kg.
Peds hypotension: SBP <70 + (2 × age in years).

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Conduction pathway
body: SA node → atria → AV node (built-in delay) → bundle of His → right/left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers.
Backup pacemakers get slower the lower you go: SA 60–100, AV junction 40–60, ventricles 20–40 per minute.
Cell properties: automaticity (fires on its own), excitability, conductivity, contractility.
Think of it as a relay race: if a runner drops out, the next one down takes over, just slower.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Reading the paper
body: Small box = 0.04 s. Large box (5 small) = 0.20 s. 5 large boxes = 1 s; 30 large boxes = 6 s.
6-second strip: count QRS complexes × 10 (works for irregular rhythms).
Regular rhythms: 1,500 ÷ small boxes between R waves, or 300 ÷ large boxes (300, 150, 100, 75, 60, 50).

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Normal values
body: P wave: rounded, upright, about 2 small boxes tall or less; one before every QRS.
PR interval: 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small boxes).
QRS: 0.04–0.12 s in this text; wider means the impulse came from, or spread abnormally through, the ventricles.
QT: normally less than half the R-to-R interval.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: Adult texts: wide = 0.12 s or more
conflicts.ri: AHA 2025 PALS uses >0.09 s as wide in children (not an RI difference, a peds one)

title: Reading a strip, same order every time
body: 1. P waves: present? upright? one per QRS?
2. PR interval: measure each one; constant, long, or changing?
3. QRS: narrow or wide? same shape?
4. Rhythm: march out R-to-R and P-to-P (calipers or paper-and-dots).
5. Rate: atrial (P) and ventricular (R); both should match the pulse.
Then look at the patient. Treat the patient, not the monitor.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Artifact
body: Static that mimics rhythms: loose or dried electrodes, patient movement, shivering, seizures, electrical interference.
Fix: dry and prep skin, fresh electrodes, still the patient, check cables.
Never call VF or asystole from the screen alone: check the patient and the leads.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Normal sinus rhythm
body: Rate 60-100 and regular. An upright P before every QRS, and all the P waves look alike.
PR 0.12-0.20 s and constant. QRS 0.04-0.12 s, all the same size and shape.
P-to-P and R-to-R are both regular and equal to each other.
The only rhythm called normal. Everything else is a dysrhythmia, which just means 'not NSR' and not necessarily dangerous.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Sinus bradycardia
body: Identical to NSR in every way except the rate is under 60.
Upright P before every QRS, PR 0.12-0.20, QRS 0.04-0.12, regular.
Normal in athletes and during sleep.
Causes: vomiting, infection, sudden cold exposure, digitalis, morphine, sedatives.
Only matters when perfusion suffers: pale cool clammy skin, dizziness, falling BP, chest pain, confusion.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Sinus tachycardia
body: Rate 101-150, regular, upright P before every QRS, PR and QRS normal.
As the rate climbs the P wave hides in the previous T wave and just makes the T look lumpy.
The cause is almost always something else: pain, fever, anemia, dehydration, hemorrhage, exercise, fear, anxiety, atropine, caffeine, nicotine, cocaine.
Treat the cause, not the number. Past 150 with no visible P waves, start thinking SVT.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Sinus arrhythmia
body: A sinus rhythm that speeds up when the patient breathes in and slows when they breathe out.
P waves upright and identical, PR 0.12-0.20, QRS normal. Only the R-to-R varies.
The longest R-to-R stays under twice the shortest, which is what separates it from a true pause.
Use a 6-second strip for the rate, since it is a moving target. Overall 60-100.
Normal in infants and children. In an adult it can hint at a diseased SA node or coronary disease.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Sinus arrest and sinus exit block
body: A whole P-QRS-T goes missing, leaving a pause.
Exit block: the SA node fired but the impulse was blocked on the way out. The pause equals exactly two or more full cycles, so the underlying rhythm stays on schedule.
Sinus arrest: the SA node never fired at all. The pause does not divide evenly and runs longer than two cycles.
Whatever escapes to end the pause may be atrial, junctional, or ventricular, so the rhythm afterward may not match the rhythm before.
Causes: MI, ischemia, hypoxia, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers, digitalis.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Premature atrial complex
body: A single early beat from an atrial site outside the SA node. One complex, not a rhythm.
Its P wave differs in size or shape from the others, or hides in the previous T wave. PR and QRS stay normal.
A pause follows. Noncompensatory (under twice the underlying R-to-R) means the SA node reset itself; compensatory (at least twice) means it ignored the early beat.
Causes: pain, fever, fear, anxiety, excitement, exercise, digitalis, atropine, nicotine, caffeine.
Harmless by itself, but frequent PACs can trigger PAT or SVT.
Always name the underlying rhythm too: 'sinus rhythm with a PAC'.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Wandering atrial pacemaker
body: The pacemaker site wanders among three or more sites above the bundle of His.
P waves change shape from beat to beat. Some may be inverted, buried, or missing, and the PR varies with them.
Irregular, rate 60-100. The same picture above 100 is multifocal atrial tachycardia.
Causes: heart or lung disease, MI, drug toxicity.
Rarely lethal, but it marks irritable atrial tissue that can progress.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: SVT, PAT, and PSVT
body: Regular, 151-250 or faster, narrow QRS, P waves usually buried in the preceding T wave.
PAT/PSVT is the same rhythm when you actually catch it starting, often kicked off by a PAC.
If you did not see it begin, call it SVT. That is the only difference between the names.
Under 151 with visible upright P waves it is sinus tachycardia instead.
At that rate the ventricles never fill, so cardiac output drops. Coronary arteries fill between beats, so the heart also starves itself.
Symptoms: weakness, dizziness, palpitations, a flip-flopping chest. Causes: caffeine, nicotine, street drugs.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Atrial flutter
body: One irritable atrial site fires 250-350 times a minute, producing sawtooth flutter waves instead of P waves.
The AV node blocks most of them, so the ventricles answer only a fraction.
Name the ratio: 4:1, 3:1, 2:1. A constant ratio gives a regular rhythm; a changing ratio is a variable conduction ratio and reads irregular.
QRS stays 0.04-0.12 s.
The ventricular rate names it: under 60 slow, 60-100 controlled, 101-150 rapid.
Atrial rate two ways: count F waves in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10, or multiply the ratio by the ventricular rate.
Causes: heart disease, MI, medication toxicity.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Atrial fibrillation
body: Every atrial cell firing at once, 350-500 or more a minute, with no organized depolarization.
No P waves and no PR interval, just a wavy fibrillatory baseline.
The giveaway is an irregularly irregular R-to-R. QRS stays narrow.
The ventricular rate names it: under 60 slow, 101-150 rapid ventricular response, over 150 uncontrolled.
The atria never fully empty, so blood pools and clots form. That is where the stroke risk comes from.
Causes: severe heart disease, valve disease, MI, stress, alcohol, caffeine.
Common in the elderly and usually not lethal. Do not confuse it with ventricular fibrillation, which is.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Wolff-Parkinson-White
body: An extra congenital pathway, the bundle of Kent, bypasses the AV node.
Three findings together: PR under 0.12 s, QRS often over 0.12 s, and a delta wave.
The delta wave is a slurred upstroke on the R wave, made by the ventricle depolarizing early through the accessory path.
Skipping the AV node is what shortens the PR, since the normal delay never happens.
Often silent and found on a routine ECG. It turns dangerous if the rate climbs to 200-300.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Junctional P waves: three positions
body: When the SA node and atria fail, the AV junction takes over at its inherent 40-60.
The impulse has to travel backward (retrograde) to reach the atria, and where it starts decides where the P wave lands.
High in the junction: inverted P before the QRS, PR under 0.12 s.
Mid-junction: atria and ventricles depolarize together, so the P is buried in the QRS and there is no PR at all.
Low in the junction: the atria fire after the ventricles, so an inverted retrograde P follows the QRS.
QRS stays 0.04-0.12 s either way, because the trip down to the ventricles still uses the normal path.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Junctional rhythm and junctional bradycardia
body: A junctional rhythm runs at the junction's inherent 40-60.
This text reserves the name 'junctional bradycardia' for under 40. Any rate under 60 is bradycardic, but only a junctional rhythm under 40 earns that label.
P inverted, buried, or retrograde. PR under 0.12 s when visible. QRS normal. Regular.
Causes: heart disease, digitalis, sedatives, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Accelerated junctional and junctional tachycardia
body: Same junctional P-wave signature, just a faster site.
61-100 is accelerated junctional. 101-150 is junctional tachycardia.
PR under 0.12 s if a P is visible, QRS 0.04-0.12 s, regular.
Causes: heart failure, acute coronary syndrome, COPD.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Premature junctional complex
body: One early beat from the junction, carrying the junctional P-wave signature.
Usually followed by a complete compensatory pause: measured around the PJC, the R-to-R is at least twice the underlying R-to-R.
Causes: pain, fever, fear, anxiety, excitement, exercise, digitalis, atropine, nicotine, caffeine, amphetamines.
Not lethal alone. Count its R wave in the rate, and name the underlying rhythm.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: First-degree AV block
body: PR over 0.20 s, constant, and every P still conducts. Nothing is dropped.
A delay rather than a true block: the impulse is just slow between the atria and the bundle of His.
Rate and rhythm belong to whatever the underlying rhythm is.
Usually benign on its own, but worth watching for progression.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Second-degree type I (Wenckebach)
body: The PR stretches a little further each beat until one QRS drops, then the cycle starts over.
The PR right after the dropped beat is back to its shortest. That reset is the signature.
P waves all alike and P-to-P regular. R-to-R irregular because of the drop.
Look for grouped beating: clusters of beats separated by pauses.
Generally the more benign of the two second-degree blocks.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Second-degree type II (Mobitz II)
body: The PR stays constant, then a QRS drops with no warning.
The underlying PR may be normal or prolonged, but it never lengthens before the drop.
P-to-P is always regular. R-to-R is regular or irregular depending on whether the ratio holds.
QRS widens if the block sits low in the bundle branches.
Name the ratio, like 3:1 or 4:1. More P waves per QRS, or a ratio that varies, means a more serious block.
Can progress to complete block. At a ventricular rate of 40 or less, perfusion fails.
Causes: MI, heart disease, drug toxicity.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Third-degree (complete) heart block
body: The atria and ventricles beat independently. Nothing crosses the AV junction.
P waves march at their own regular rate, QRS at its own regular rate, with no relationship between the two.
The PR appears to change constantly because there is no true PR at all.
Key discriminator: nothing is dropped. Second-degree blocks drop beats; third-degree never does.
Atrial rate usually 60-100. The ventricular escape usually runs 20-40.
A narrow QRS means the escape came from the junction. A wide one means it came from ventricular tissue, which is slower and less reliable.
Life threatening. Causes: MI, severe heart disease.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Premature ventricular complex
body: One early beat from below the bundle of His. Wide and bizarre, over 0.12 s, often deflecting opposite the underlying QRS.
No P wave of its own, and the T wave points opposite the QRS.
Usually a complete compensatory pause: measured around the PVC, the R-to-R equals twice the underlying R-to-R.
Unifocal PVCs all look alike. Multifocal ones differ in shape and mean more irritability.
Frequency names them: bigeminy every other beat, trigeminy every third, quadrigeminy every fourth, a couplet is two in a row, three or more is a run of VT.
Not every PVC makes a pulse, so count the pulse rather than trusting the monitor.
Warning signs: more than six a minute, multifocal, couplets, runs, or R-on-T.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: R-on-T phenomenon
body: A PVC lands on the previous T wave, during repolarization.
That is the vulnerable period, when some cells have recovered enough to fire again and others have not.
A strong enough stimulus there can tip the rhythm into VT or VF.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Ventricular tachycardia
body: Three or more PVCs in a row. Usually a single site, 101-250, wide QRS over 0.12 s, with a very regular R-to-R.
P waves, if visible at all, belong to the underlying rhythm. PR and P-to-P are not measurable.
Under 30 seconds is unsustained, or a run. Over 30 seconds is sustained.
The same wide look at 41-100 is accelerated idioventricular rhythm, not VT.
May have a pulse or not. Pulseless VT is treated as cardiac arrest.
Causes: MI, advanced heart disease, severe ischemia, electrical shock, epinephrine, digitalis.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Torsades de pointes
body: A polymorphic VT whose QRS amplitude swells and shrinks, twisting around the baseline. The name means 'twisting of the points'.
Rate often 120-240, most commonly 170-190. Wide QRS, usually regular R-to-R.
Typically preceded by a long QT, meaning more than half the R-to-R of that complex.
Telling it apart from ordinary VT matters because the treatment differs.
Causes: low magnesium, a long QT, and QT-prolonging drugs such as methadone.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Ventricular fibrillation
body: Many ventricular sites firing chaotically at once. No P waves, no QRS, no measurable rate.
Only a chaotic wavy line. The ventricles quiver instead of contracting, so there is no pulse.
Coarse VF has taller waves and more cells still responding. Fine VF has lower amplitude and fewer.
CPR and defibrillation immediately.
Causes: severe heart disease, electrical shock, drug toxicity, hypoxia, severe electrolyte imbalance.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Idioventricular, accelerated idioventricular, and agonal
body: The ventricles are the last pacemaker standing. No P waves, no PR, wide bizarre QRS over 0.12 s.
Under 40 is idioventricular. 41-100 is accelerated idioventricular. Under 20 is agonal, the dying heart.
R-to-R may be irregular. The complexes get wider and flatter as the heart fails.
Lethal. Seen in acute cardiopulmonary events and at the end stage of advanced heart disease.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Ventricular standstill and asystole
body: Ventricular standstill: P waves present and regular, but no QRS at all. Atrial rate 60-100, ventricular rate zero.
Asystole: no electrical activity anywhere, a flat line.
Neither produces a pulse, and both need treatment immediately.
Standstill can follow third-degree block, a massive MI, or ventricular rupture.
Before calling asystole, check the patient, confirm in a second lead, and check the leads and the gain.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Escape beats
body: A late beat from a backup site when the SA node pauses or the rate falls. The heart's safety net, not irritability.
That is the mirror image of a premature beat: early beats mean an irritable site jumping the queue, late beats mean a backup site rescuing a gap.
Named by where it comes from: atrial (upright P, PR 0.12-0.20), junctional (inverted, buried, or retrograde P), ventricular (wide, P usually hidden).
The complex that ends a sinus arrest or exit block is an escape beat.
If the backup site has to keep firing, a single escape beat becomes an escape rhythm.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Aberrantly conducted complexes
body: A beat that starts above the bundle of His but takes an abnormal route through the bundle branches.
One ventricle depolarizes later than the other, so for that one beat the QRS looks like a bundle branch block.
Usually wide, and it may deflect opposite the underlying rhythm or be narrower or shorter than its neighbors.
Individual complexes, not whole rhythms. Hard to separate from a PVC or a true BBB.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias, 5th ed. (lecture outlines)

title: Bundle branch block
body: Not a true block. One bundle branch is interrupted, so its ventricle depolarizes late.
Two separate depolarizations show up as one notched or widened QRS over 0.12 s. The notch is the classic 'rabbit ears'.
Rate, rhythm, P waves and PR all come from the underlying rhythm. The block does not change any of them.
Name the underlying rhythm first: 'sinus rhythm with a bundle branch block'.
A 12-lead showing V1 and V6 is what tells right from left.
Causes: heart disease, MI. A new left bundle branch block with chest pain is worked up as a possible STEMI.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: Pulseless electrical activity
body: Any organized rhythm on the monitor with no palpable pulse. The older name was electromechanical dissociation.
It usually looks bradycardic, and the QRS may be wide or narrow. Almost any rhythm can present this way.
Only touching the patient finds it, because the monitor looks fine.
Treat as cardiac arrest: CPR and epinephrine, and hunt the reversible causes.
Common causes: hypovolemia, hypoxia, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, or muscle too damaged to contract.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 1 mg every 3–5 min
conflicts.ri: RI 3.03A: 1 mg every 5 min, max 5 doses for non-shockable rhythms

title: Pacemakers and implanted defibrillators
body: Pacer spikes: vertical lines before the P (atrial), QRS (ventricular), or both (dual chamber).
Failure to capture: spike with no complex after it. Failure to sense: spikes fire at the wrong time.
ICD: may shock the patient on its own; you can touch them safely during CPR.
Don't place defibrillator pads directly over an implanted device.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

title: 12-lead: where's the infarct?
body: Inferior (II, III, aVF): usually the RCA. Get a right-sided lead (V4R) to check for RV infarct.
Septal (V1–V2) and anterior (V3–V4): LAD.
Lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6): circumflex.
Posterior: ST depression in V1–V3 with tall R waves.
STEMI: ST elevation in 2 or more contiguous leads (V2–V3: ≥2 mm men, ≥1.5 mm women; ≥1 mm elsewhere).

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: Textbook: use nitro cautiously with RV involvement
conflicts.ri: RI 3.02: no nitro in RV infarction; if hypotension follows nitro, stop it and give fluid

title: Treating the big rhythms
body: Unstable = hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure.
Unstable tachycardia: synchronized cardioversion. Unstable bradycardia: atropine, then pacing or pressors.
Stable regular narrow tachycardia: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine.
Pulseless VF/VT: defibrillate; epinephrine and amiodarone or lidocaine.

source.doc: Introduction to Basic Cardiac Dysrhythmias (text + lecture slides)

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 6 mg rapid IV push with flush, then 12 mg
conflicts.ri: RI 3.06A: 12 mg first, may repeat × 1

conflicts.nremt: AHA: 1 mg every 3–5 min, max 3 mg
conflicts.ri: RI 3.05A: 0.5–1 mg every 3–5 min to HR >60, max 3 mg

conflicts.nremt: Textbook: rate control per protocol
conflicts.ri: RI 3.06A: diltiazem only after medical control; max 20 mg first dose

title: Who counts as a child
body: Infant: under about 1 year (newborns follow neonatal guidelines). Child: 1 year to puberty. Puberty onward: adult BLS.
Kids rarely arrest from the heart itself: it's usually respiratory failure or shock first, so fix breathing early.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

title: High-quality pediatric CPR (2025)
body: Rate 100–120/min; depth at least ⅓ of the chest (about 1.5 in infants, 2 in children); full recoil.
Pauses under 10 s; pulse check no longer than 10 s.
No advanced airway: 30:2 with one rescuer, 15:2 with two (before puberty).
Advanced airway: continuous compressions, 1 breath every 2–3 s (20–30/min).
Breathing inadequately but has a pulse: 1 breath every 2–3 s; reassess pulse every 2 min.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

conflicts.nremt: 15:2 with two rescuers until an advanced airway is placed
conflicts.ri: RI 3.03P: continuous compressions prioritized; ventilate 20–30/min, avoid over-ventilation

title: Hand technique (changed in 2025)
body: Infants: heel of 1 hand on the sternum, or 2 thumbs with hands encircling the chest.
The 2-finger technique was removed: it rarely reached proper depth.
Children: 1 or 2 hands, whichever gets the depth.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

title: Choking (changed in 2025)
body: Mild (coughing, making sounds): let them cough and watch.
Infant, severe: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts (heel of hand). No abdominal thrusts.
Child, severe: 5 back blows, then 5 abdominal thrusts, repeated.
Goes unresponsive: start CPR with compressions, no pulse check; look in the mouth before breaths. No blind finger sweeps.

source.doc: AHA/AAP 2025 Guidelines Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support

conflicts.nremt: AHA 2025: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
conflicts.ri: RI 7.02: abdominal thrusts (Heimlich) only

title: Defibrillation in kids
body: AED on a child under 8: use a pediatric attenuator/pads. None available? An adult AED is still better than no shock.
Manual: 2 J/kg first, 4 J/kg second, then ≥4 J/kg up to 10 J/kg or the adult dose.
Pads: largest that fit with 1–2 cm between them; front-back or front-side both OK.
One shock, then straight back to compressions.

conflicts.ri: RI 3.03P matches: 2 → 4 → ≥4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg or adult dose)

title: Pediatric arrest drugs
body: Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (0.1 mg/mL = 0.1 mL/kg), max 1 mg, every 3–5 min. Non-shockable: give it as early as possible.
Shock-refractory VF/pVT: amiodarone 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg), up to 3 doses (max 150 mg after the first), or lidocaine 1 mg/kg.
No routine sodium bicarbonate or calcium (except special cases like hyperkalemia or sodium-channel blocker overdose).
Reversible causes: the Hs and Ts.

title: Pediatric bradycardia
body: Bradycardia with poor perfusion often means arrest is coming.
Oxygenate and ventilate first. HR under 60 with poor perfusion despite that: start CPR.
Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (max 1 mg). Atropine 0.02 mg/kg (min 0.1 mg, max single 0.5 mg, may repeat once) for vagal cause or AV block.
Consider pacing.

title: Pediatric tachycardia
body: Probable sinus tach: P waves present, variable R-R, infant under 220, child under 180. Treat the cause.
Probable SVT: no normal P waves, fixed R-R, infant ≥220, child ≥180, abrupt start.
Narrow = 0.09 s or less. Stable SVT: vagal maneuvers, then adenosine 0.1 mg/kg (max 6 mg), then 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg).
Unstable: adenosine if IV is ready, or synchronized cardioversion 0.5–1 J/kg, then 2 J/kg.
Wide and unstable: cardioversion; get expert consultation before more drugs.

body: Isotonic crystalloid; balanced (LR) or normal saline both acceptable.
Septic shock: 10 or 20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment after each.

title: Angina vs heart attack
body: RECOGNITION (RI 3.02): chest pain or discomfort consistent with a cardiac cause, "or other known or suspected anginal equivalent including fatigue, nausea, dyspnea, dizziness (common symptoms in women)". RI names the atypical presentation in the protocol itself rather than leaving it to a footnote.

STEMI CRITERIA (RI 3.02, verbatim): "ST elevation in ≥2 contiguous leads of ≥ 2mm in males or ≥ 1.5mm in females in leads V2-V3 and/or of ≥1 mm in other contiguous chest leads or the limb leads." The male and female thresholds differ, and only in V2–V3.

POSTERIOR MI: ST depression greater than 1 mm in V1–V3 with a dominant R wave (R/S ratio above 1) in V2 and upright T waves. New left bundle branch block counts too, but "must be evaluated in context".
ANGINA VS INFARCTION is a distinction of duration and reversibility, not of field treatment — ACS covers the whole spectrum of acute myocardial ischaemia and the protocol is the same.
RI 3.02 ACTIONS: acquire a multi-lead (≥12 lead) ECG and transmit it to Medical Control; limit on-scene time to 10 minutes or less.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 3.02 Chest Pain — Acute Coronary Syndrome — STEMI

title: Chest pain, ACS and STEMI care (RI 3.02)
body: Recognition is broader than chest pain: any anginal equivalent counts — fatigue, nausea, dyspnea, dizziness. RI names these as common presentations IN WOMEN.
STEMI criteria, and the thresholds differ by sex: ST elevation in ≥ 2 contiguous leads of ≥ 2 mm in MALES or ≥ 1.5 mm in FEMALES in V2–V3, and/or ≥ 1 mm in other contiguous chest or limb leads.
Posterior MI is the one you miss by not looking for it: ST DEPRESSION > 1 mm in V1–V3 with a dominant R wave (R/S ratio > 1) in V2 and upright T waves.
New-onset left bundle branch block must be evaluated in context — it is not automatically a STEMI.
Aspirin 81 mg × 4 orally, chewed, unless allergic or unable to swallow safely. That is 324 mg.
A patient prescribed nitroglycerin with an SBP ≥ 100 may take 0.3/0.4 mg SL of THEIR OWN supply, repeatable every 5 minutes to a maximum of 3 doses while the SBP stays ≥ 100.
Acquire a multi-lead (≥ 12-lead) ECG and TRANSMIT it to medical control at the nearest PCI-capable facility for help with interpretation.

If the ECG suggests STEMI, three things happen together: limit on-scene time to ≤ 10 MINUTES, triage to the nearest PCI-capable facility, and give immediate CODE STEMI notification with the patient's name, date of birth and ID number if available.
If the first ECG is not diagnostic but suspicion stays high, obtain SERIAL ECGs rather than settling for the first one.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Cardiogenic shock
body: The pump cannot move enough blood, most often after an infarction.

RI 3.01 RECOGNITION puts the findings together: respiratory distress, orthopnea, bilateral crackles, jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, diaphoresis, hypotension, shock, chest pain. Crackles and distended neck veins are what separate this from hypovolemia — the tank is full and the pump has stopped moving it.
RI 3.01 ROUTES IT OUT: "If the patient is hypotensive or has signs of cardiogenic shock or poor perfusion, manage per the age appropriate General Shock and Hypotension Protocol" (2.20A for adults).
Oxygen to the RI 1.01 target of 94–99%, upright as the pressure allows, keep them warm, and get ALS moving early.
Note the pressure floors in 3.01: CPAP needs an SBP of at least 90, nitroglycerin needs above 100. A cardiogenic-shock patient is usually under both.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 3.01 Acute Decompensated Heart Failure / Pulmonary Edema, with 2.20A General Shock and Hypotension

title: Acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema (RI 3.01)
body: Recognition: respiratory distress, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, BILATERAL crackles, jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, diaphoresis, hypotension or shock, and chest pain or discomfort.
Position first: sit the patient upright as tolerated and as the blood pressure allows.
CPAP up to 10 cmH2O for respiratory distress, crackles, or an SpO2 < 92% — gated on an SBP ≥ 90. This is available at the EMT level, which surprises people.
Aspirin 81 mg × 4 chewed, as in ACS.
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL (tablet, lingual spray or powder) every 5 minutes while the SBP is > 100. Note the threshold is 100, not 90.

A specific and unusual standing order: if transport is ≥ 30 minutes, the patient already takes ORAL furosemide, and they are normotensive (SBP ≥ 100), you may give their own daily dose as FUROSEMIDE IV (maximum 80 mg) instead of the oral route they normally use.
Midazolam 1–2 mg IV for CPAP mask compliance requires MEDICAL CONTROL authorization.

Two off-ramps: chest pain or discomfort routes to the Chest Pain / ACS / STEMI Protocol, and hypotension or signs of cardiogenic shock route to the age-appropriate General Shock and Hypotension Protocol.

At the Paramedic level the drug changes shape — a nitroglycerin IV infusion starting at 100 mcg/minute, titrated rapidly downward as symptoms improve or the MAP drops 30%, discontinued if the SBP falls below 100.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Hypertensive emergency
body: THE NUMBERS (NHLBI High Blood Pressure): the hypertensive crisis category is "Higher than 180 systolic pressure OR Higher than 120 diastolic pressure" — either one, not both.

WHAT MAKES IT AN EMERGENCY (JNC 7 Express): acute target-organ damage. Patients "with marked BP elevations and acute target-organ damage" need hospitalisation and parenteral therapy; patients "with markedly elevated BP but without acute target organ damage" are an urgency and usually do not.

EXAMPLES JNC 7 NAMES as acute target-organ damage: encephalopathy, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, pulmonary oedema, eclampsia, stroke, head trauma, life-threatening arterial bleeding, and aortic dissection.
So the number alone does not make the emergency. A chronically hypertensive patient can sit above 180 and be entirely well; what changes the category is evidence that an organ is suffering right now.

FIELD CARE: head elevated, IV access, rapid transport. RI has no hypertensive-emergency protocol — its only SBP ≥ 185 / DBP ≥ 110 figures belong to protocol 2.13 IV Thrombolytics, which is about eligibility for stroke thrombolysis, not about treating pressure.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — JNC 7 Express: The Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee on Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure

note: Two sources, deliberately. JNC 7 Express draws the emergency/urgency line at acute target-organ damage but gives no numeric threshold for the crisis categories; the 180/120 figures come from the NHLBI High Blood Pressure page, which gives the numbers but never mentions organ damage. Neither document carries both halves.

title: Aortic dissection
body: Sudden tearing pain in the chest or between the shoulder blades, classically migrating as the dissection extends.

JNC 7 Express lists aortic dissection among the forms of acute target-organ damage that make a markedly elevated blood pressure a hypertensive EMERGENCY rather than an urgency — which is the federal basis for the link between uncontrolled hypertension and dissection.

RI names it only once, inside a differential list alongside myocardial infarction and myocarditis. There is no RI dissection protocol: recognition and rapid transport are the whole of the prehospital job.
Treat it as a hypertensive emergency in the making and move — this is not a patient to work up on scene.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — JNC 7 Express: The Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee on Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Treatment of High Blood Pressure

note: The "check blood pressure in both arms" manoeuvre is standard physical examination and is stated by neither JNC 7 nor RI. It is retained on the matching question as exam technique and flagged there, not cited to either source.

title: Cardiac devices
body: Pacemaker and ICD: a palpable bump under the skin, usually upper chest. An ICD can discharge while you are touching the patient; it will not harm you.
Wearable defibrillator vest: it can shock on its own, and it talks — follow its voice prompts.

VENTRICULAR ASSIST DEVICE: RI 3.08 exists specifically for these patients. Continuous-flow devices mean there may be no palpable pulse and no reliable blood pressure, so the usual perfusion checks mislead.
With a VAD, the device team is part of the assessment. Follow RI 3.08 and contact them — they know the pump, its alarms, and its controller in a way no field protocol can substitute for.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 3.08 Care of the Patient with a Ventricular Assist Device (VAD)

title: Adult cardiac arrest, the RI scene rules (3.03A)
body: Airway: a blindly inserted airway device — i-Gel, King airway, laryngeal mask — SHALL be the initial advanced airway of choice in every adult arrest. Not an endotracheal tube.
Continuous waveform capnography confirming advanced airway placement is MANDATORY, and must be monitored and documented. RI uses the word mandatory.

The scene rule that defines RI practice: regardless of how close the hospital is, run the resuscitation AT THE SCENE for a minimum of 30 MINUTES before moving the patient to the ambulance or transporting.
That 30-minute rule has exactly three exceptions: a concern for EMS personnel safety, a confirmed pregnancy beyond 20 weeks gestation, or a traumatic etiology for the arrest.

After 30 minutes, four findings argue for staying and continuing on scene: organized electrical activity, a shockable rhythm, an EtCO2 ≥ 20 mmHg, or signs of life such as purposeful movement or eye opening during CPR.
BLS crews should request ALS if available rather than transporting early.
On ROSC, move to the age-appropriate Post Cardiac Arrest Care Protocol.

Destination is not simply the nearest hospital: a patient with STEMI, hemodynamic instability (MAP < 65 or SBP < 90), or electrical instability (recurrent VF/VT, or bradycardia recurring despite pacing or drugs) goes to a PCI-capable facility.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: IV fluids: what RI carries and when
body: RI names a fluid of choice for each job, and they are different fluids. 0.9% saline for keep-vein-open purposes and LIMITED boluses; lactated Ringer's for SIGNIFICANT fluid resuscitation in shock and burn injury, unless a protocol says otherwise.
KVO rates are specified: 20–30 mL/hour for adults, 10–20 mL/hour for pediatrics.
Pediatric maintenance fluid is the 4-2-1 rule, stated in RI 1.01 §15: 4 mL/kg for the first 10 kg, plus 2 mL/kg for the second 10 kg, plus 1 mL/kg for every additional kg.
Dextrose 10% is carried as a premixed 10% solution yielding 10 g per 100 mL (appendix 09.02) — which is the 0.1 g/mL you use in every peds glucose calculation.
Appendix 09.02 "Standard Concentrations for IV Admixtures" is the authority for what a mixed bag should read, and it also names which level may carry each and whether a pump is required.
An intermittent needle therapy device — a saline lock — may be placed instead of an infusing IV when appropriate.
IO access is interchangeable with IV throughout the RI protocols, and any reference to the IV route of medication administration includes the IO route.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

The previous card taught isotonic/hypotonic/hypertonic and the "water chasing salt" analogy — that is A&P mechanism, and no public-domain source available this session states it (OpenStax A&P 2e is CC BY-NC-SA and therefore unusable here). What RI DOES state is which fluid to hang for which job, at what rate, which is the operationally useful half. The tonicity explanation is deferred to Tier 3.

title: Administration sets and drip math
body: Microdrip: 60 gtt/mL (small volumes, kids, medications). Macrodrip: 10–15 gtt/mL (volume).
gtt/min = (mL × drip factor) ÷ minutes.

title: Catheter size
body: Gauge: the bigger the number, the smaller the catheter.
Large bore (14–18) for trauma and volume; 20–24 for kids, older adults, and fragile veins.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

title: IV complications
body: Infiltration: swelling, cool pale skin, slowed flow. Stop, remove, restart in the other arm.
Thrombophlebitis: red, warm, tender vein. Stop and restart elsewhere.
Air embolism, catheter shear, arterial puncture, vasovagal reaction.
Circulatory overload: crackles, JVD, dyspnea. Slow to TKO, sit them up, notify.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 13: Vascular Access and Medication Administration (lecture slides)

title: Intraosseous access
body: IO is indicated when a patient needs rapid vascular access and peripheral IV access is unavailable, or when secondary access is needed in a critically ill or injured patient.
In cardiac arrest, an IO placed SUPERIOR TO THE DIAPHRAGM may be used as the PRIMARY vascular access — not a fallback. And placing it must not interrupt chest compressions.
Every medication in the RI protocols that is routinely given IV can be given IO.

Sites follow the DEVICE, not a memorised landmark: use the FDA-approved insertion sites for the device you carry, which may include the proximal or distal tibia, the proximal humerus, or the sternum. RI directs you to the manufacturer's recommendations for both use and anatomic placement.
Spring-loaded devices for STERNAL placement are the one exception RI excludes outright.
Confirming placement: the device generally stands without support and infused fluid does not infiltrate. Aspirating marrow confirms placement, but NOT aspirating marrow proves nothing either way.
An awake, alert patient gets intramedullary anesthesia — 2% cardiac lidocaine pushed slowly through the device, 20–50 mg for an adult and 0.5 mg/kg for a child.
Flush 10 mL of normal saline before first use, and flush again after every medication. Continuous resuscitation fluid needs a pressure infuser bag; vasopressors need an infusion pump.
Document the device size and type, number of attempts, anatomic location, whether anesthetic was used, and any complications.

title: Controlled substance schedules
body: Schedule I: high potential for abuse, NO currently accepted medical use in the United States, and a lack of accepted safety for use under medical supervision. That third clause is why nothing in Schedule I is carried on an ambulance.

Schedule II: high potential for abuse, but a currently accepted medical use — possibly with severe restrictions — and abuse may lead to severe psychological or physical dependence. Fentanyl is listed here, as DEA code 9801 (21 CFR 1308.12).
Schedule III: abuse potential less than I and II, accepted medical use, and abuse may lead to moderate or low physical dependence or high psychological dependence.

Schedule IV: low abuse potential relative to Schedule III, accepted medical use, limited dependence relative to Schedule III. All three EMS benzodiazepines are listed here — diazepam 2765, lorazepam 2885, midazolam 2884 (21 CFR 1308.14).
Schedule V: low abuse potential relative to Schedule IV, accepted medical use, limited dependence relative to Schedule IV.

The pattern to hold: abuse potential falls as the number rises, and every schedule except I has an accepted medical use. The statute requires all three findings to be made before a substance is placed in a schedule.

Note the split: the STATUTE (21 U.S.C. 812(b)) sets the test for each schedule; the REGULATION (21 CFR 1308) lists which substances are actually in them. A drug can be rescheduled by regulation without the statute changing.

source.doc: 21 U.S.C. § 812(b) — Controlled Substances Act, findings required for each schedule

note: Findings sourced to 21 U.S.C. 812(b). The individual substance placements were verified in 21 CFR 1308 via the eCFR API — fentanyl 9801 under 1308.12 (Schedule II), diazepam 2765 / lorazepam 2885 / midazolam 2884 under 1308.14 (Schedule IV): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-1308 . title: Autonomic receptors
body: Alpha-1: vasoconstriction. Beta-1: heart rate and contractility up. Beta-2: bronchodilation.
Memory hook: 1 heart, 2 lungs.
Parasympathetic (acetylcholine): slows the heart, makes secretions. Anticholinergics (atropine) block it.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 12: Principles of Pharmacology (lecture slides)

title: Routes, fastest to slowest
body: IV/IO fastest; then inhaled, intranasal, IM, subcutaneous, oral.
Absorption depends on blood flow: a shocky patient absorbs IM and SQ poorly.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 12: Principles of Pharmacology (lecture slides)

title: Key electrolytes
body: Sodium: water balance. Potassium: heart rhythm (high or low K both cause dysrhythmias).
Calcium: muscle contraction and clotting. Magnesium: nerve and muscle function.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 8: Pathophysiology (lecture slides)

title: Acid–base in one card
body: Respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation (CO₂ builds). Respiratory alkalosis: hyperventilation.
Metabolic acidosis: DKA, shock (lactic acid), overdose. Metabolic alkalosis: vomiting, antacids.
The body compensates: fast deep breathing (Kussmaul) blows off CO₂ in metabolic acidosis.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 8: Pathophysiology (lecture slides)

title: Cellular injury
body: Hypoxia is the most common cause of cell injury.
Other causes: chemicals, infection, immune reactions, genetics, nutrition, physical agents.
Unchecked shock leads to MODS: organ failures cascading hours to days later.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 8: Pathophysiology (lecture slides)

title: Routine patient care, the RI sequence
body: Approach the scene cautiously and assess scene safety first. If a hazard is identified, request assistance and use PPE as indicated; if the scene is unsafe, STAGE until the hazards or threats are mitigated.

Use standard precautions for every patient contact. RI defines these as gloves, gowns, mask, and eye protection or a face shield, chosen by the anticipated degree of exposure — then institute transmission-based precautions on top as indicated.
Hand hygiene before AND after each patient contact, for every patient, no exceptions.
Bring all necessary equipment to the patient rather than making trips back to the truck.
Use the Major Incident Protocol when the patient count or resource need calls for it.

Determine whether the patient meets pediatric or adult criteria by age — that single decision routes you to the A or P half of nearly every protocol that follows. RI defines a pediatric patient as under 16 years of age.

At or below 36 kg / 80 lb, use a pediatric dosing device (Broselow, Handtevy or other). If using the Broselow tape and the patient is taller than the tape, keep dosing by weight until age 16 or a total body weight of 50 kg. Some special-needs patients stay on pediatric protocols regardless of age.

Destination is chosen by capability, not distance: RI 1.01 Table 2 names the Point of Entry facilities — ACS-verified Level 1 trauma (Rhode Island Hospital, Hasbro for pediatrics), ABA-verified burn centers, comprehensive versus primary stroke centers and acute stroke ready hospitals, and the primary PCI-capable hospitals.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Transmission-based precautions (RI Table 1)
body: CONTACT: standard precautions plus gloves for patient contact and for touching the patient's environment or belongings, gowns and gloves changed after every patient, surfaces and reusable equipment cleaned and disinfected, and strict hand washing. Applies to norovirus, rotavirus, enterovirus, C. difficile, acute diarrhea of unknown cause, RSV, adenovirus, multidrug-resistant organisms including MRSA and VRE, scabies and head lice, and undressed or inadequately contained wound drainage.

DROPLET: standard precautions plus a surgical mask for any clinician in the back of the ambulance or within 3 feet of the patient, AND a surgical mask or non-rebreather on the patient. Applies to influenza, parainfluenza, RSV, bronchiolitis, meningitis, mumps, pertussis, and upper respiratory infections including unidentified ones.

AIRBORNE: standard precautions plus an N95 respirator OR a powered air purifying respirator (PAPR). Applies to tuberculosis or symptoms consistent with pulmonary TB — night sweats, fever, hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss — plus measles, varicella, disseminated shingles, vesicular rash, SARS-CoV-2 and Mpox.
Some pathogens need a COMBINATION: RI gives varicella as the example, requiring standard plus airborne plus contact precautions together.
C. difficile and acute diarrhea of unknown cause require SOAP AND WATER hand hygiene specifically — alcohol gel does not kill the spores. This is the detail most often missed.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Four ways breathing fails
body: NHLBI groups the causes by what the failure interrupts rather than by anatomy. AIR CANNOT GET IN: weakness after a stroke, collapsed airways, or something blocking the windpipe.
AIR CANNOT GET OUT: asthma narrowing the airways, or COPD filling them with mucus.

THE LUNG CANNOT HOLD AIR OR EXCHANGE IT: a collapsed lung or air leaking into the space around it after chest injury; or fluid in the lungs from pneumonia, ARDS, drowning, heart failure or severe head injury, making transfer between air sacs and blood harder.
THE PUMP FAILS: spinal cord injury, muscular dystrophy, poor blood flow to the diaphragm, cardiogenic shock or sepsis leaving the breathing muscles unable to do the work.
THE CONTROLLER FAILS: in opioid overdose "the brain doesn’t respond to rising carbon dioxide", so CO2 climbs while oxygen falls.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Respiratory Failure — Causes and Risk Factors

note: Rebuilt on NHLBI’s own grouping. Worth knowing what that page does NOT do: it never uses the terms hypoxemic, hypercapnic, V/Q mismatch, hypoventilation or impaired diffusion. Those belong to the textbook framing and have no federal source yet, so this card teaches NHLBI’s categories instead of renaming them.

title: Alveoli, surfactant, and the V/Q match
body: Type I alveolar cells do the gas exchange; Type II make surfactant and new Type I cells.
Surfactant lowers surface tension so alveoli stay open; collapsed or fluid-filled alveoli can't exchange gas.
Chronic hypoxia leads the body to overproduce RBCs (polycythemia); thicker blood strains the right heart (cor pulmonale).

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

verify: Type I and Type II alveolar cells, surfactant and the V/Q match are textbook anatomy and physiology. NHLBI’s respiratory pages do not carry them at this depth, and RI carries no anatomy at all. Needs the Tier 3 A&P sourcing decision.

title: CO2 retention and hypoxic drive
body: Chronic CO2 retention makes the brain's CO2-sensing drive less responsive over time.
Hypoxic drive is a backup: the brain breathes based on low O2 instead of high CO2.
Heavy supplemental O2 can blunt that backup drive and depress respirations, but never withhold O2 from a patient who needs it; support ventilation instead.

title: Hypo/hyperventilation and the I:E ratio
body: Hypoventilation traps CO2 and causes respiratory acidosis.
Hyperventilation (tachypnea without a physiologic O2 demand) drops CO2 and causes respiratory alkalosis; can mimic a panic attack.
Normal expiration lasts about twice as long as inspiration (I:E ratio); prolonged in asthma, shortened in tachypnea.

That says nothing about normal spontaneous breathing, so citing it here would misattribute. The respiratory acidosis/alkalosis half needs the pathophysiology sourcing decision.

title: COPD: chronic bronchitis vs emphysema
body: CHRONIC BRONCHITIS (NHLBI): "caused by repeated or constant irritation and inflammation in the lining of the airways", with "a lot of thick mucus" forming in the airways, making it hard to breathe.

EMPHYSEMA (NHLBI): "develops when there is damage to the walls between many of the air sacs in the lungs." NHLBI does not attribute that damage to lost surfactant, and neither should you — surfactant appears nowhere in its account of COPD.

NEITHER IS "THE COMMON ONE". NHLBI says most people with COPD have a mix of both, in varying proportions. Treating them as two separate diseases to tell apart is a textbook convenience, not what walks through the door.
FIELD PICTURE (RI 2.08A recognition): shortness of breath, pursed lip breathing, wheezing or rhonchi, prolonged expiratory phase, accessory muscle use, increased rate and effort, fever, cough.
Dry lungs — pair with pulmonary edema’s wet lungs for the breath-sound gut check, and treat the patient rather than the sounds.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — COPD

note: Two corrections on re-sourcing. The previous card said emphysema is "alveolar wall destruction from lost surfactant" and "the most common form of COPD". NHLBI supports neither claim: it gives no cause for the wall damage, never mentions surfactant in connection with COPD, and states that most patients have both conditions mixed.

title: Asthma: the reversible triad
body: THE THREE COMPONENTS (EPR-3): acute symptoms "usually arise from bronchial smooth muscle contraction (bronchoconstriction)"; as disease becomes more persistent, airflow is further limited by airway edema, "mucus hypersecretion and the formation of inspissated mucus plugs", and structural remodelling.

REVERSIBLE — BUT NOT ALWAYS FULLY. EPR-3 describes "widespread but variable airflow obstruction that is often reversible", and warns that "Reversibility of airflow limitation may be incomplete in some patients with asthma." Airway remodelling can leave permanent change that current therapy does not reverse.

SILENT CHEST (RI 2.08A, NOTES, verbatim): "A ‘silent chest’ in the asthmatic patient is a pre-respiratory arrest indicator." It is not improvement — there is no longer enough airflow to make a wheeze.

RI 2.08A LADDER: albuterol 2.5–5 mg with ipratropium 500 mcg on the first dose via SVN, up to 4 doses; methylprednisolone 125 mg IV; CPAP 5–10 cmH2O for a patient not responding to initial therapy; epinephrine 1:1,000 0.3 mg IM for the asthmatic in extremis, on Medical Control at AEMT-C.
RI also warns that asthmatics drop their pressure after going onto positive pressure, because preload falls — and that a rising EtCO2 is acceptable rather than something to hyperventilate away.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Expert Panel Report 3, Section 2: Definition, Pathophysiology and Pathogenesis of Asthma, and Natural History of Asthma (2007)

note: The previous card called all three components reversible without qualification. EPR-3 is more careful: obstruction is "often reversible" and reversibility "may be incomplete in some patients".

title: Pulmonary edema: wet lungs
body: RECOGNITION (RI 3.01, verbatim list): respiratory distress, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, bilateral crackles on auscultation, jugular venous distention, peripheral edema, diaphoresis, hypotension, shock, chest pain or discomfort.
Fluid floods the alveoli and lung tissue, so gas exchange falls — the wet-lung counterpart to COPD’s dry lungs.

RI 3.01 LADDER: upright as blood pressure allows; CPAP up to 10 cmH2O for distress, crackles or SpO2 under 92% provided the SBP is at least 90; nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL every 5 minutes once the SBP is above 100.
AEMT-C ADDITION: on a transport of 30 minutes or more, for a normotensive patient who takes oral furosemide, their own daily dose (maximum 80 mg) may be given IV instead.
Note the two different pressure floors in one protocol: CPAP needs SBP ≥ 90, nitroglycerin needs SBP > 100. They are not the same number and the protocol does not treat them as such.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026) — 3.01 Acute Decompensated Heart Failure / Pulmonary Edema

title: Pneumothorax vs pleural effusion
body: ONE SPACE, TWO PROBLEMS (NHLBI): pleural effusion and pneumothorax occur when injury or illness causes "fluid, pus, blood, air, or other gases to build up in the pleural space". Air gives a pneumothorax; fluid gives an effusion.

WHO GETS A SPONTANEOUS PNEUMOTHORAX (NHLBI): "Men, especially those who are taller than average, are more likely than women to have a spontaneous pneumothorax, often without underlying lung disease." Pneumothorax is commonest at ages 15–34 and again over 55, and smoking tobacco or marijuana raises the risk.
EFFUSION MECHANISM (NHLBI): fluid collects when it "enters the pleural space faster than the body can reabsorb it", which is why heart, kidney or liver failure produce them.
AT THE BEDSIDE the percussion note separates them: air is hyperresonant, fluid is dull. Breath sounds fall on the affected side either way, and an effusion patient often prefers sitting up.
Both sit on RI 2.08A’s own differential for respiratory distress, alongside asthma, COPD, anaphylaxis, aspiration, pneumonia, pulmonary embolus, CHF, hyperventilation and inhaled toxin.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Pleural Disorders — Causes and Risk Factors

note: The previous card said "tall thin young males". NHLBI says men "taller than average", gives two age peaks (15–34 and over 55) rather than one young band, and does not mention build. The percussion findings are standard physical-examination technique and are not stated by NHLBI or RI; they are retained as exam technique rather than cited to either.

title: Pulmonary embolism
body: MECHANISM (NHLBI): a clot forms in a deep vein — "usually in the lower leg, thigh, or pelvis" — and "Pulmonary embolism occurs when a clot breaks loose and travels through the bloodstream to the lungs", where it "blocks blood flow to the lungs".

RISK FACTORS NHLBI NAMES: prolonged immobility, including "after surgery or while traveling long distances"; surgery or trauma; a history of blood clots; cancer and its treatment; obesity; increasing age; family history; infection and inflammation. Before menopause, women are at higher risk than men.

FIELD SIGNS: sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, tachypnea, pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia, sometimes haemoptysis. Breath sounds are usually present and equal, which is what separates it from a pneumothorax on examination.
On RI 2.08A’s differential for respiratory distress as "pulmonary embolus" — there is no RI prehospital treatment protocol specific to PE, so care is supportive and the priority is recognising it.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Venous Thromboembolism — Causes and Risk Factors

Neither appears on the NHLBI venous thromboembolism pages checked, so both are held out pending their own source. Pregnancy appears only in that page’s meta description and not its body, so it is left out too.

title: Croup vs epiglottitis vs bronchiolitis
body: RI 2.08P SETS THE AGES AND THE FINDINGS. Bronchiolitis: under 2 years, peaking 3–6 months, with poor feeding or fussiness, increasing coryza and congestion, low-grade fever, cough, fine crackles and fine diffuse wheezing.
CROUP: 6 months to 6 years, peaking under 4, following an upper respiratory infection, with low-grade fever, coryza, a "barking" cough and varying respiratory distress.
ASTHMA/RAD: over 2 years, with wheezing, cough, chest tightness and a prolonged expiratory phase.
EPIGLOTTITIS: over 2 years, fever, toxic or ill appearing, favouring an upright position, drooling, stridor. Avoid airway manipulation and suctioning — let secretions drain, keep the child calm.

RI TREATMENT for stridor at rest: nebulised epinephrine (2.25% solution 0.5 mL in 3 mL NS, or 1 mg/mL 5 mg), may repeat once; dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM/IV to a 10 mg maximum. Oxygen if the SpO2 is 92% or below.
Always consider a foreign body first in a child who went from eating to short of breath — the one cause that needs no fever and no prodrome.

title: Naming abnormal breath sounds
body: Crackles (rales): fine, crackling, air moving through fluid in the alveoli.
Rhonchi: lower-pitched, secretions/mucus in the larger airways.
Stridor: high-pitched, inspiratory, upper-airway obstruction.
Wheezing: high-pitched, typically expiratory, bronchoconstriction/inflammation.
Pleural friction rub: squeaking/grating, inflamed pleural linings rubbing together.

source.doc: AEMT textbook Ch 17: Respiratory Emergencies (lecture slides)

verify: RI uses stridor, wheeze, rhonchi and crackles throughout but never defines them. No federal source checked defines the set either. The terms are standard nomenclature; the definitions need a source before this card can be cited.

title: Oxygen targets and CPAP
body: OXYGEN TARGET (RI 1.01): titrate to the LOWEST concentration that maintains an SpO2 of 94–99%. More is not better — the target has a ceiling as well as a floor.

CPAP INDICATIONS (procedure 7.01): acute decompensated heart failure and cardiogenic pulmonary edema; and respiratory distress or hypoxic respiratory failure associated with asthma, COPD, pneumonia or near-drowning.

CPAP CONTRAINDICATIONS (7.01), worth memorising as a list: respiratory arrest or agonal breathing; inability to maintain the airway; GCS < 8 or inability to follow commands; vomiting or active upper GI hemorrhage; facial fractures or deformities preventing a mask seal; pneumothorax.
Technique (7.01): start at ZERO pressure and titrate upward based on pathology and the patient's response, to a maximum of 10 cmH2O.
In heart failure specifically (RI 3.01), CPAP up to 10 cmH2O is indicated for respiratory distress, crackles, or SpO2 < 92% — provided the SBP is ≥ 90.
CPAP is first-line for cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and 7.01 states it has been shown to reduce the need for endotracheal intubation.
If the patient fights the mask, RI 3.01 and 2.08A both allow midazolam 1–2 mg IV for mask compliance — but only with MEDICAL CONTROL authorization.

title: Insulin and glucagon: the two directions
body: INSULIN (NIDDK): a hormone made by the pancreas that helps glucose get INTO your cells to be used for energy. Glucose comes from food, and the body also makes its own.

Diabetes is one of two failures of that single step — the body "doesn't make enough, or any, insulin, or doesn't use insulin properly." Either way glucose stays in the blood instead of entering cells.

TYPE 1: the immune system attacks and destroys the pancreatic cells that make insulin, so the body makes little or none. Usually diagnosed in children and young adults, but it can appear at any age. These patients "need to take insulin every day to stay alive" — which is why a missed dose is a genuine emergency rather than an oversight.
TYPE 2: the cells do not use insulin properly. The pancreas may still be making insulin, just not enough to overcome that. Same end result, different mechanism.

GLUCAGON runs the other direction — it raises blood glucose by mobilising the liver's glycogen stores. RI 2.10A carries it for the hypoglycemic patient who cannot safely swallow: glucagon 1 mg (1 unit) IM, or glucagon nasal powder (Baqsimi) 3 mg IN.

The catch worth knowing: glucagon only works if there IS glycogen to mobilise. In starvation, chronic alcohol use, or prolonged hypoglycemia the stores are already empty, and the FDA label for glucagon says so outright. A patient who does not respond is not a patient who needs a second dose — they need dextrose.

That is why RI routes by capability rather than by drug preference: awake and able to swallow gets oral glucose, not alert or vomiting gets glucagon at the EMT level, and the advanced levels go to D10W because it works regardless of liver stores.

source.doc: NIDDK (NIH) — What Is Diabetes?

title: Low versus high: telling the two diabetic emergencies apart
body: ONSET is the first discriminator. NIDDK: hypoglycemia symptoms "tend to come on quickly and can vary from person to person." CDC on DKA: it "usually develops slowly," with early thirst and urination before anything dramatic. Fast and scattered means low; slow and building means high.

SKIN is the second. RI 2.10A recognition gives hypoglycemia as "anxiety, altered mental status, diaphoresis, seizures, tachycardia" — diaphoretic, sweaty. DKA it gives as "warm dry skin." Wet and confused versus dry and confused.
SEVERE HYPOGLYCEMIA (NIDDK) is defined by what the patient can no longer do: "You may lose consciousness, have a seizure." It "needs to be treated right away."
Hypoglycemia can also happen during SLEEP and stay low for several hours — which is how a patient ends up found down in the morning with no witnessed onset at all.

THE 15-15 APPROACH (NIDDK) for the awake patient: 15 to 20 grams of glucose or fast carbohydrate, then recheck. Their examples: four glucose tablets, one tube of glucose gel, or half a cup (4 oz) of fruit juice — specifically NOT low-calorie or reduced-sugar, which is the trap in a diabetic household.
RI 2.10A uses the same structure: 15 g oral glucose solution, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low.
DKA's objective anchors, for contrast: acetone odor on the breath and an EtCO2 ≤ 29 mmHg (RI 2.10A), against hyperglycemia the CDC pins at > 250 mg/dL with acidosis and ketones.
If you cannot get a glucose reading at all, RI says treat on presentation — the patient's mental status and ability to take oral glucose decide the route, not a number you do not have.

THE THREE BANDS (RI 2.10A), which are the numbers that change care: ≤60 mg/dL treat — oral glucose if awake and alert, glucagon 1 mg IM or Baqsimi 3 mg IN if not alert or vomiting, and at AEMT-C thiamine 200 mg then D10W 250 mL over 5 minutes; 60–249 mg/dL recheck only if the condition changes; ≥250 mg/dL normal saline 500 mL IV if dehydrated without CHF, repeat as needed, then 150 mL/hr. RI names no "normal" band at all.

There is no published normal nonfasting range to quote. NIDDK gives diagnostic thresholds — fasting 99 mg/dL or below normal, 100–125 prediabetes, 126 or above diabetes — and no normal value for a random glucose. The "70–120" figure common in AEMT texts has no federal or state source, so this deck teaches the action bands instead.

title: DKA: mechanism, field recognition, and the HHS gap
body: MECHANISM (CDC): without enough insulin, blood sugar cannot get into the cells to be used as energy. The liver falls back on breaking down FAT for fuel, and that process produces acids called ketones. Produced too fast, they build to dangerous levels. The patient is starving at the cellular level while drowning in sugar.
Most common in type 1 diabetes, but type 2 patients develop it too — so "they are type 2" does not rule it out.
DKA is sometimes the FIRST noticeable sign of diabetes in someone never diagnosed. No history of diabetes is not a reason to drop it off your list.
EARLY (CDC): very thirsty, urinating much more than usual. These are the osmotic diuresis showing up before anything dramatic does.

LATER, AND FAST (CDC): fast deep breathing, dry skin and mouth, flushed face, fruity-smelling breath, headache, muscle stiffness or aches, profound tiredness, nausea and vomiting, stomach pain. The abdominal pain is worth holding onto — DKA is on the differential for the vomiting patient with belly pain.
RI FIELD RECOGNITION (2.10A), stated differently and worth knowing in its own words: "warm dry skin, tachycardia, rapid shallow breathing, hypotension/shock, acetone odor on breath, EtCO2 ≤29 mmHg."

That EtCO2 ≤ 29 mmHg is the number to carry. It is the capnography signature of blowing off CO2 to compensate for a metabolic acidosis, and it is the one objective DKA finding RI gives you that does not depend on smelling anything.

NUMBERS (CDC): check ketones once blood sugar is 250 mg/dL or above. Emergency care if the sugar STAYS at 300 mg/dL or above, the breath smells fruity, vomiting prevents keeping anything down, breathing is difficult, or several DKA signs appear together.
The MMWR case definition is tighter still: uncontrolled hyperglycemia (> 250 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis, AND raised ketones — all three, not any one.

PRECIPITANTS (CDC): illness; a missed insulin dose, clogged pump, or wrong dose; heart attack or stroke; physical injury such as a crash; alcohol or drug use; and certain medicines including some diuretics and corticosteroids. Two of those — MI and stroke — mean DKA can be the presentation of a second emergency you have not found yet.

WHAT RI DOES ABOUT IT: nothing DKA-specific. Protocol 2.10A routes by blood glucose and mental status only, and its treatment arm exists to raise a LOW sugar. There is no prehospital standing order for hyperglycemia at any RI level — the care is routine patient care and transport.

Tier 2 specimen. Sourced to CDC for mechanism, symptom progression and thresholds, and to RI 2.10A for field recognition — two independent public-domain authorities that agree on substance.

HHS/HHNS is deliberately NOT described. It has no usable public-domain source: NIDDK has no page (zero hits for "ketoacidosis" across every NIDDK and NHLBI page that resolves), CDC has only incidental MMWR and COVID-era ED-utilization mentions, RI returns zero hits for HHNS/HHS/hyperosmolar, and the MedlinePlus health topics link out to /ency/ (A.D.A.M. Medical Encyclopedia, copyrighted) and to Mayo Clinic. Describing HHS would mean citing a source that does not state it. The card teaches the verifiable fact instead — that RI never branches on the distinction — and the conflicts block carries it as a national-vs-RI divergence.

Second conflict recorded rather than smoothed: CDC says "fast, deep breathing" and RI 2.10A says "rapid shallow breathing" for the same sign. Both quoted verbatim. Kussmaul respirations are classically deep, so RI's wording is the outlier, but it is what the protocol says and a student reading 2.10A will see it.

title: Treating low glucose: RI routes the dose by mental status
body: RI 2.10A does not route by glucose number alone — it routes by bG AND whether the patient can safely swallow. That is the structure of the table.
bG ≤ 60 and the patient is AWAKE AND ALERT: oral glucose solution, 15 g PO. Recheck in 15 minutes. Repeat the dose if the bG is still ≤ 60. Same at every level, EMT through Paramedic.
bG ≤ 60 and the patient is NOT alert to verbal stimuli, or is nauseated or vomiting — at the EMT level: glucagon 1 mg (1 unit) IM, or glucagon nasal powder (Baqsimi) 3 mg IN. No oral anything.
Same patient at the advanced level: thiamine 200 mg IV/IM FIRST, then D10W 250 mL (25 g) IV over 5 minutes, repeatable in 5 minutes if the bG is still < 60.
If IV access cannot be established at the advanced level, fall back to the same glucagon 1 mg IM or Baqsimi 3 mg IN.
bG 60–249: recheck only if the condition changes. No treatment.

Thiamine before dextrose is not ritual — it is on the 50% dextrose federal label as a contraindication in alcohol withdrawal, because glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. RI reserves thiamine for patients with a history of alcohol abuse or who appear malnourished.

Recognition split: hypoglycemia shows anxiety, altered mental status, diaphoresis, seizures, tachycardia. DKA shows warm DRY skin, tachycardia, rapid shallow breathing, hypotension or shock, an acetone odour, and an EtCO2 ≤ 29 mmHg.

title: Sickle cell crisis (RI 2.23)
body: Sickle cell crisis occurs in patients with sickle cell disease, a family of diseases that includes the hemolytic anemia known as sickle cell anemia.
The usual presentation is ACUTE PAIN — sharp, intense, stabbing or throbbing — anywhere, but most often in the joints, lower back, legs, arms, abdomen or chest.
It is not only pain. Patients may present with stroke, priapism, acute chest syndrome (fever, chest pain, hypoxemia, respiratory symptoms), skin ulcerations, or ocular manifestations.
In young children, add three more: dactylitis (swollen digits), splenic sequestration (enlarged spleen, pallor, hypotension) and aplastic crisis (bone marrow shutdown, noticed as pallor).
Suspected stroke goes to the Ischemic Stroke Protocol, not this one.
Consider supplemental oxygen; consider analgesia per the age-appropriate Patient Comfort Protocol; and normal saline 20 mL/kg IV if the patient appears dehydrated.
Transport to the nearest appropriate facility, and consider a Pediatric Specialty Care Hospital for children.

RI's own note explains the mechanism: most manifestations are secondary to VASCULAR OCCLUSION and inflammation. Crises can be precipitated by physical and environmental factors — treat any precipitant you can identify.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Clotting gone two ways
body: TOO MUCH (NHLBI): venous thromboembolism is "a condition that occurs when a blood clot forms in a vein." VTE is the umbrella covering two presentations — deep vein thrombosis, where the clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg, and pulmonary embolism, where it reaches the lung.
TOO LITTLE (NHLBI): thrombocytopenia "develops when the platelet count in your blood is too low." Platelets are what stop bleeding when you are injured, so a low count means trouble stopping it.
Where that bleeding shows: "inside your body, underneath your skin, or on the surface of your skin." The internal one is the one you will miss.

NHLBI's own emergency criterion is a field-usable rule: call 911 for "bleeding that does not stop when you apply pressure." And they note a patient "may not have serious bleeding until your platelet count is very low" — so a normal-looking patient is not reassurance.

RI appendix 09.04, the Blood Thinner Chart, splits the drugs by the same two mechanisms. ANTIPLATELETS: aspirin (salicylate), clopidogrel (Plavix), prasugrel (Effient), ticagrelor (Brilinta), dipyridamole (Persantine, Aggrenox).
ANTICOAGULANTS: warfarin (Coumadin), heparin, enoxaparin (Lovenox), dabigatran (Pradaxa), rivaroxaban (Xarelto), apixaban (Eliquis), fondaparinux (Arixtra).

The distinction is not academic. Antiplatelets stop platelets clumping; anticoagulants interrupt the clotting cascade. RI protocols ask you to "attempt to obtain information related to use of antiplatelet or anticoagulants" because the answer changes what the receiving facility can do.

VTE closes the loop back to shock and arrest: RI 2.20A lists "history of DVT, risk factors for pulmonary embolus" among the obstructive shock findings, and pulmonary embolism is the second T — Thrombosis — in RI 3.03A's reversible causes of cardiac arrest.
