note: Built from two NHLBI health topics — Venous Thromboembolism for the clotting side and Platelet Disorders: Thrombocytopenia (https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/thrombocytopenia) for the bleeding side — plus RI appendix 09.04. The NHLBI landing pages are thin; only what they state directly is used here. Hemophilia was not included: NHLBI returns 404 at /health/hemophilia and RI contains no instance of it.

title: Anemia in the field
body: WHAT IT IS (NHLBI): anemia "develops when your blood produces a lower-than-normal amount of healthy red blood cells," so "your body does not get enough oxygen-rich blood." The problem is carrying capacity, not saturation.

THE FIELD TRAP, and the reason this card exists. RI procedure 7.16 states it outright: "Patients with anemia have a reduced level of functional Hb, however this limited amount of functional Hb may be well saturated with oxygen, so the patient may have a normal SpO2 in spite of having a reduced oxygen carrying capacity and potential hypoxia."

Read that again as a number problem: SpO2 is a PERCENTAGE of the hemoglobin you have. Halve the hemoglobin and the percentage does not move. A 100% reading on half the carrying capacity is still half the oxygen.

TYPES (NHLBI): iron-deficiency, vitamin B12-deficiency, hemolytic, and aplastic. Onset can be sudden or gradual, and causes include diet, medicines the patient takes, or another medical condition. It can also be chronic — a patient can live at a hemoglobin that would alarm you.

RI names anemia among the underlying causes to consider for a tachycardic patient (protocol 3.06A), alongside sepsis and dehydration. A heart rate that will not settle has a reason, and this is one of them.

The sickle cell connection is RI's own: protocol 2.23 describes sickle cell disease as "a family of diseases including a hemolytic anemia known as sickle cell anemia." Your sickle cell patient IS an anemia patient, with all of the above applying.

Other things 7.16 says will fool the oximeter, worth holding together: poor perfusion or vasoconstriction in shock, hypothermia, irregular rhythms or tachycardia, nail polish or prosthetic nails, and external light. The device reports confidence it has not earned.

source.doc: NHLBI (NIH) — Anemia: What Is Anemia?

note: The central pearl is quoted verbatim from RI procedure 7.16 (Pulse Oximetry) rather than paraphrased, because the mechanism is easy to garble and the protocol states it precisely. NHLBI supplies the definition and the type list; the landing page is thin, so nothing beyond what it states is asserted.

title: Adrenal insufficiency (RI 2.03)
body: Who: a history of adrenal insufficiency or Addison's disease, HIV/AIDS, or sepsis.

The history that is easy to miss: LONG-TERM STEROID USE for asthma, COPD, rheumatoid arthritis or organ transplant, and the use of antifungal agents. Ask the medication list, not just the diagnosis list.
Presentation: hypotension, nausea, vomiting, dehydration, abdominal pain. It looks like undifferentiated shock, which is why RI 2.20A tells you to think of it.
Maintain and promote normothermia with blankets and by raising the ambient temperature.
Check a blood glucose and treat per the age-appropriate Diabetic Emergencies Protocol — these patients go low.
Manage the hypotension per the age-appropriate General Shock and Hypotension Protocol.

The definitive drug is a steroid: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV is PREFERRED (2 mg/kg, 100 mg maximum for pediatrics), or methylprednisolone 125 mg IV (2 mg/kg, max 60 mg peds), or dexamethasone 10 mg IV (0.3 mg/kg, max 10 mg peds).
Note the pediatric maxima run in the opposite order to the adult doses: hydrocortisone caps at 100 mg but methylprednisolone caps at 60 mg.

source.doc: RI Statewide EMS Protocols v2026.02 (eff. 6/1/2026)

title: Blood, in four jobs and three organs
body: Plasma carries everything; RBCs carry oxygen; WBCs fight infection; platelets start clots.
Bone marrow makes blood cells; the liver makes clotting factors and filters blood; the spleen filters and recycles RBCs.
ABO plus Rh typing is why mismatched transfusions can cause rapid, severe reactions.

title: Reading the patient before the glucometer
body: Warm, dry skin plus Kussmaul respirations plus fruity breath points to hyperglycemia/DKA.
Moist, pale skin plus rapid weak pulse plus normal-to-rapid shallow breathing points to hypoglycemia.
Never assume altered mental status is just a known diabetic's baseline; check a blood glucose every time.
Sickle cell clues on scene: swelling of fingers/toes, jaundice, priapism, pain isolated vs. whole-body.
